The [[Tour de France]] is an annual [[Road bicycle racing|road bicycle race]] held over 23&nbsp;days in July. Established in [[1903 Tour de France|1903]] by newspaper ''[[L'Équipe|L'Auto]]'', the Tour is the best-known and most prestigious of cycling's three "[[Grand Tour (cycling)|Grand Tours]]", the others being the [[Giro d'Italia]] and the [[Vuelta a España]].<ref>{{cite book |url=http://www.uci.ch/templates/UCI/UCI1/layout.asp?MenuId=MTk0Nw&LangId=1 |title=FAQ |publisher=[[Union Cycliste Internationale]] |access-date=17 August 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090723024909/http://www.uci.ch/templates/UCI/UCI1/layout.asp?MenuId=MTk0Nw&LangId=1 |archive-date=23 July 2009 }}</ref> The race usually covers approximately 3,500 kilometres (2,200&nbsp;mi), passing through France and neighbouring countries.<ref>{{cite book|author=Dauncey, Hugh |author2=Hare, Geoff  |year= 2003 |title=Tour de France: 1903–2003 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=54pAJY6Ix8YC |publisher=[[Routledge]] |isbn=978-0-7146-5362-4 |page=149}}</ref> The race is broken into day-long stages, and individual finishing times for each stage are totalled to determine the overall winner at the end of the race. The course changes every year, but has finished in Paris every year except [[2024 Tour de France|2024]], when it finished in [[Nice]]. Since [[1975 Tour de France|1975]], it has finished along the [[Champs-Élysées]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cyclingnews.com/features/tour-de-france-gallery-history-on-the-champs-elysees/ |title=Tour de France Gallery: History on the Champs-Élysées |publisher=Cycling News |date=21 July 2013 |access-date=18 July 2021 }}</ref>

The rider with the lowest aggregate time at the end of each day wears the yellow jersey, representing the leader of the [[general classification in the Tour de France|general classification]]. There are other jerseys: the green jersey, worn by the leader of the [[points classification in the Tour de France|points classification]]; the polka dot jersey, worn by the leader of the [[Mountains classification in the Tour de France|mountains classification]]; and the white jersey, worn by the leader of the [[Young rider classification in the Tour de France|young rider classification]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.cyclingweekly.com/news/racing/tour-de-france/tour-de-france-the-jerseys-59552 |title=Tour de France jerseys: Yellow, green, white and polka-dot explained |work=Cycling Weekly |date=24 August 2020 |access-date=18 July 2021 |first=Tom |last=Bonville-Ginn }}</ref>

Sixty-four individual cyclists from 15 countries have won a combined total of 106 Tours, the [[2026 Tour de France|most recent]] winner being Slovenian [[Tadej Pogačar]].<ref name="pog1">{{Cite news |last=Whittle |first=Jeremy |date=2026-07-26 |title=Relentless Tadej Pogacar wins fifth Tour de France to equal record |url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/jul/26/relentless-tadej-pogacar-wins-fifth-tour-de-france-to-equal-record |access-date=2026-07-30 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> Pogačar, [[Jacques Anquetil]], [[Eddy Merckx]], [[Bernard Hinault]] and [[Miguel Induráin]] hold the record for the most victories at five each,{{efn|name=Armstrong}} with Induráin being the only one to win five consecutive Tours. Winners have ranged in age from 19 ([[Henri Cornet]], [[1904 Tour de France|1904]]) to 36 years ([[Firmin Lambot]], [[1922 Tour de France|1922]]).<ref>{{cite news|url=https://abcnews.go.com/Travel/story?id=8011893&page=1 |first=Christopher |last=Scholiansky |title=Will He? Won't He? Can Armstrong Win Tour de France? |publisher=[[American Broadcasting Company]] |date=6 July 2009 |access-date=14 August 2009 }}</ref> The most common nationality among winners is French (36 Tours won by 21 cyclists), followed by Belgian (18 Tours won by 10 cyclists) and Spanish (12 Tours won by 7 cyclists).<ref>{{cite web |url=http://netstorage.lequipe.fr/ASO/cyclisme/le-tour/2017/histoire/TDF17_GH_Interactif-PROD.pdf |title=Guide Historique 2017|publisher=[[Tour de France]] |access-date=9 October 2017 }}</ref>

==History==
The [[Tour de France]] was established in 1903 by the newspaper ''[[L'Auto]]'', in an attempt to increase its sales. The first race was won by Frenchman [[Maurice Garin]]. He won again the next year, but was disqualified after allegations that he had been transported by car or rail. [[Henri Cornet]] became the winner after the dispute was settled, and is the youngest to win the Tour. Following the scandals in 1904, the scoring system was changed from being time-based to a point-based system, in which the cyclist who has the fewest points at the end of the race is victorious. This system lasted until [[1912 Tour de France|1912]], when the time-based system was reintroduced. French cyclists won the first six Tours, before [[François Faber]] of Luxembourg won in [[1909 Tour de France|1909]], the first non-Frenchman to win.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/in_depth/2001/tour_de_france/1364736.stm |title=1903–1914: Pioneers and 'assassins' |publisher=BBC Sport |date=5 June 2001 |access-date=20 August 2009 }}</ref>

Belgian riders were more successful before and after the [[First World War]], which caused the Tour to be suspended from 1915 to 1918. In the 1920s, trade teams dominated the Tour, and cyclists such as [[Nicolas Frantz]] won the Tour with the [[Alcyon (cycling team)|Alcyon]] team. When Alcyon cyclist [[Maurice De Waele]] won the Tour in [[1929 Tour de France|1929]] while ill, the organisers decided to introduce national teams the following year, to stop team tactics from undermining the race. Because of the [[Second World War]], the Tour de France was [[Tour de France during World War II|suspended]] from 1940 to 1946.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/in_depth/2001/tour_de_france/1364739.stm |title=1930–1939: Adapt to survive |publisher=BBC Sport |date=5 June 2001 |access-date=20 August 2009 }}</ref>

[[File:Desmet gif.gif|thumb|upright|alt=A woolen yellow jersey with writing on it|The yellow jersey ({{langx|fr|maillot jaune}}) of [[1963 Tour de France|1963]], worn by [[General classification in the Tour de France|general classification]] leader [[Gilbert Desmet]] of {{UCI team code|Groene Leeuw|1963}}]]

After the [[Second World War]], no one dominated the Tour until [[Louison Bobet]], who won three consecutive Tours from [[1953 Tour de France|1953]] to [[1955 Tour de France|1955]]—he was the first person to achieve this feat.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/in_depth/2001/tour_de_france/1364738.stm |title=1947–1956: Post-war rivalries |publisher=BBC Sport |date=5 June 2001 |access-date=20 August 2009 }}</ref> This was bettered by the French cyclist [[Jacques Anquetil]], who won four successive Tours from [[1961 Tour de France|1961]] to [[1964 Tour de France|1964]]. Anquetil, who also won in [[1957 Tour de France|1957]], became the first to win five Tours.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/in_depth/2001/tour_de_france/1364732.stm |title=1957–1966: Anquetil 5–0 Poulidor |publisher=BBC Sport |date=5 June 2001 |access-date=20 August 2009 }}</ref> Anquetil's five victories were matched when Belgian cyclist [[Eddy Merckx]] won four successive Tours from [[1969 Tour de France|1969]] to [[1972 Tour de France|1972]] and the [[1974 Tour de France|1974]] Tour. Merckx is the only person to have won the general, points and king of the mountains classifications in the same Tour, which he achieved in 1969.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/in_depth/2001/tour_de_france/1364740.stm |title=1967–1977: Tragedy before a Cannibal's feast |publisher=BBC Sport |date=5 June 2001|access-date=18 August 2009 }}</ref>

Merckx looked to be heading for a record sixth Tour victory in [[1975 Tour de France|1975]], but [[Bernard Thévenet]] beat him, becoming the first French winner in seven years. Thévenet won again in [[1977 Tour de France|1977]], but he was eclipsed in the following years by fellow Frenchman [[Bernard Hinault]], who won consecutive Tours in [[1978 Tour de France|1978]] and [[1979 Tour de France|1979]]. Hinault won the Tour at his first attempt in 1978, becoming one of 11 cyclists (including Anquetil, Merckx, [[Hugo Koblet]] and [[Fausto Coppi]]) who managed to do so.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/in_depth/2001/tour_de_france/1364742.stm |title=1978–1984: The Badger's golden era |publisher=BBC Sport |date=5 June 2001 |access-date=19 August 2009 }}</ref> In [[1980 Tour de France|1980]], the Tour was won by [[Joop Zoetemelk]], after Hinault had to pull out because of tendinitis.<ref>{{cite book|first=Vic |last=Armijo |year=1999 |title=The complete idiot's guide to cycling |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=w4cYE5flGIMC |publisher=Alpha Books |isbn=0-02-862929-9 |page=28}}</ref> Hinault returned and won in [[1981 Tour de France|1981]] and 1982. Hinault sat out the Tour in [[1983 Tour de France|1983]], and [[Laurent Fignon]], another Frenchman, achieved victory. Fignon won again the following year, beating Hinault, before Hinault recovered in [[1985 Tour de France|1985]] to win his fifth Tour.

American [[Greg LeMond]] became the first non-European to win the Tour in [[1986 Tour de France|1986]]. LeMond won again in 1989 to win the Tour by finishing eight seconds ahead of Fignon, the smallest winning margin in the Tour's history. LeMond also won in 1990.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/in_depth/2001/tour_de_france/1364744.stm |title=1985–1990: American, Irishman and Spaniard |publisher=BBC Sport |date=5 June 2001 |access-date=22 August 2009 }}</ref> In [[1991 Tour de France|1991]], Spaniard [[Miguel Induráin]] won his first Tour. Induráin came to dominate the Tour, winning four more Tours consecutively—making him the first person to win five consecutive Tours.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/in_depth/2001/tour_de_france/1364745.stm |title=1991–1995: Big Mig's masterclass |publisher=BBC Sport |date=5 June 2001 |access-date=22 August 2009 }}</ref> He tried to win a record sixth Tour in [[1996 Tour de France|1996]], but was beaten by [[Bjarne Riis]], who later admitted to using [[Erythropoietin]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601085&sid=aG.4N3TyZIVM&refer=europe |title=Riis, Tour de France Champ, Says He Took Banned Drugs |publisher=Bloomberg L.P. |date=25 May 2007 |access-date=31 August 2009 |first=Alex |last=Duff |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070930082459/http://www.bloomberg.com/apps/news?pid=20601085&sid=aG.4N3TyZIVM&refer=europe |archive-date=30 September 2007 }}</ref> [[Jan Ullrich]] and [[Marco Pantani]] won in [[1997 Tour de France|1997]] and [[1998 Tour de France|1998]], respectively, but Pantani's victory was overshadowed by [[Festina affair|doping scandals]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/in_depth/2001/tour_de_france/1364747.stm |title=1996–2000: Doping and the great recovery |publisher=BBC Sport |date=5 June 2001 |access-date=22 August 2009 }}</ref>

The [[1999 Tour de France|1999]] Tour saw the first of [[Lance Armstrong]]'s seven consecutive victories.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport/hi/english/static/in_depth/other_sports/2002/tour_de_france/statistics/overall.stm |title=Overall standings 2002 |publisher=BBC Sport |date=28 July 2002 |access-date=20 August 2009 |archive-date=24 July 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080724230325/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport/hi/english/static/in_depth/other_sports/2002/tour_de_france/statistics/overall.stm |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/other_sports/cycling/4712583.stm |title=Armstrong seals seventh Tour win |publisher=[[BBC Sport]] |date=24 July 2005 |access-date=20 August 2009 }}</ref> He was stripped of his titles in October 2012, when it emerged he had used [[History of Lance Armstrong doping allegations|performance-enhancing drugs]] throughout much of his career, including the Tour de France victories.<ref name="Armstrong">{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/20008520 |title=Armstrong stripped of all seven Tour de France wins by UCI |publisher=BBC Sport |date=22 October 2012 |access-date=22 October 2012 }}</ref> [[Floyd Landis]] won the Tour in [[2006 Tour de France|2006]], but was later stripped of his title after a [[Floyd Landis doping case|failed drug test]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2006/08/05/sports/05cnd-landis.ready.html?_r=1 |title=Backup Sample on Landis is positive |work=The New York Times |first=Juliet |last=Macur |date=5 August 2006 |access-date=20 August 2009 }}</ref> [[Óscar Pereiro]] was subsequently awarded the victory. [[Alberto Contador]] won the [[2007 Tour de France|2007]] Tour with the {{UCI team code|DSC|2007}}. The 2007 Tour was also marred by [[Doping at the 2007 Tour de France|doping scandals]], thus Contador was unable to defend his title in [[2008 Tour de France|2008]], as his [[Astana (cycling team)|Astana]] team was banned for its part in the controversy. Fellow Spaniard [[Carlos Sastre]] of {{UCI team code|CSC|2008a}} won.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/other_sports/cycling/7527797.stm |title=Sastre wins Tour de France crown |publisher=BBC Sport |date=27 July 2008 |access-date=8 September 2009 }}</ref> Contador and Astana returned in [[2009 Tour de France|2009]] to regain the title. He won the Tour again in [[2010 Tour de France|2010]], but was later stripped of his title after he was found guilty of doping. Runner-up [[Andy Schleck]] was awarded the victory.

[[Cadel Evans]] became the first Australian to win the Tour in [[2011 Tour de France|2011]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/14266126 |title=Tour de France: Cavendish wins historic green jersey |publisher=BBC Sport |date=24 July 2011 |access-date=24 July 2011 }}</ref> In 2012, [[Bradley Wiggins]] became the first British cyclist to win the Tour.<ref name="wiggins">{{cite web|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/18946960 |title=Bradley Wiggins wins Tour de France for Team Sky |publisher=BBC Sport |date=22 July 2012 |access-date=22 July 2012 }}</ref> [[Chris Froome]] became the second successive British winner in [[2013 Tour de France|2013]], which was the 100th edition of the race.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/23399875 |title=Tour de France:Chris Froome wins 100th edition of race |publisher=[[BBC Sport]] |date=22 July 2013 |access-date=31 May 2015 |first=Anna |last=Thompson }}</ref> He could not defend his title the following year, as he crashed out in stage 5, with [[Vincenzo Nibali]] winning his first Tour.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/28515493 |title=Tour de France: Vincenzo Nibali completes race victory |publisher=BBC Sport |date=27 July 2014 |access-date=31 May 2015 }}</ref> Froome regained the title in [[2015 Tour de France|2015]] and successfully defended it in [[2016 Tour de France|2016]], the first rider in over 20 years to do so.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/36879128 |title=Tour de France 2016: Chris Froome completes third race victory |publisher=BBC Sport |date=24 July 2016 |access-date=17 November 2016}}</ref> Froome won the Tour for a third consecutive year in [[2017 Tour de France|2017]].<ref name="froome-2017">{{cite news|last=Fletcher|first=Paul|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/40695072 |title=Tour de France 2017: Chris Froome wins yellow jersey for the fourth time |publisher=[[BBC Sport]] |date=23 July 2017 |access-date=26 September 2017}}</ref> Froome's teammate, [[Geraint Thomas]], was the winner of the [[2018 Tour de France|2018 race]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/44998961 |title=Geraint Thomas wins as Chris Froome finishes third |publisher=BBC Sport |date=29 July 2018 |access-date=13 April 2020 |first=Peter |last=Scrivener }}</ref> [[Egan Bernal]] won in [[2019 Tour de France|2019]], becoming the first Colombian cyclist to win the Tour, finishing ahead of his teammate Thomas.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2019/jul/29/egan-bernal-tour-de-france-winner-colombia |title=Egan Bernal rides into history and puts Colombian cycling on the map |work=The Guardian|location=London |date=29 July 2019 |access-date=13 April 2020 |first=Jeremy |last=Whittle }}</ref>

The 2020 Tour was postponed, to start on 29 August, following the French government's extension of a ban on mass gatherings after the worldwide [[Coronavirus disease 2019|COVID-19]] outbreak.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/52275648|title=Tour de France to go ahead at end of August after coronavirus delay|date=15 April 2020|publisher=BBC Sport|access-date=15 April 2020}}</ref> This was the first time since the end of World War II that the Tour was not held in July.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lindsey |first1=Joe |title=The Tour de France Goes Virtual |date=29 June 2020 |url=https://www.outsideonline.com/2415248/tour-de-france-virtual-online-coronavirus |publisher=Outside |access-date=30 June 2020}}</ref> It was won by [[Tadej Pogačar]], who became the first Slovenian rider to win the race as well as one of the youngest winners in Tour history. He repeated as champion in the 2021 edition. The following year, [[Jonas Vingegaard]] became the first Danish rider since 1996 to win the race. Vingegaard won again in 2023, by 7 minutes and 29 seconds from Pogačar.<ref name="vingegaard">{{cite news |last=Bevan |first=Chris |date=23 July 2023 |title=Tour de France 2023: Jonas Vingegaard retains title as Jordi Meeus claims surprise win in Paris |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/66285026 |access-date=23 July 2023 |publisher=BBC Sport}}</ref> Pogačar won again in 2024 and became the first person to win the Giro and Tour in the same year since Pantani in 1998.<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/articles/cy08gkr4m9no |title=Pogacar seals third Tour de France with stage 21 win |publisher=BBC Sport |date=21 July 2024 |access-date=21 July 2024 |first=Joe |last=Rindl }}</ref> Pogačar retained his title in 2025, beating Vingegaard by 4 minutes and 24 seconds.<ref name="pog">{{Cite news |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/cycling/articles/ckgyjg5lj78o |title=Van Aert wins final stage as Pogacar seals Tour title |date=27 July 2025 |access-date=28 July 2025 |first=Ben |last=Collins }}</ref> Pogačar again retained his title in 2026, beating Remco Evenepoel by 6 minutes and 26 seconds.<ref name=pog1 />

===Multiple winners===

The following riders have won the Tour de France on more than one occasion.

[[Alberto Contador]] won three Tours, but was stripped of one following an anti-doping violation.{{ref label|Contador|D|b}}

[[Lance Armstrong]] was removed from the head of the list after having all seven of his Tour victories stripped when he was found guilty of repeated doping offences.
